title: A Plan Others Can Believe
segs: Chapter 6. A Plan Others Can Believe.

Anaya's first manager taught her to make plans that looked like railway timetables. Features went down the side and months went across the top. Each feature got a bar that began on one date and ended on another. She had made about a dozen of these. She couldn't remember one that had come true.

The dates were usually wrong, but that wasn't the main flaw. Each bar was a promise to build something, and none of them was a promise that the thing would help. When the dates slipped, the plan turned into a list of broken commitments. When a feature turned out not to matter, it became a list of broken commitments to the wrong thing.

After the founders agreed in principle to the privacy tool, Anaya started a new plan on a clean page, with a different structure. In this chapter we look at that structure and the goals attached to it. We also meet the people who could stop it, and a meeting that tested the plan before it began.
The case: a plan with no dates.

The strategy from the last chapter was still only a sentence. For engineers, compliance staff and founders to act on it, it needed three things. It needed an order of work. It needed a way to tell whether the work succeeded. And it needed an account of who could get in the way.
The sections below take those three needs in turn. Then comes a fourth step: a meeting where colleagues were asked to suppose the project had already failed.
The outcome roadmap.
A roadmap in the form Anaya adopted has three columns and no calendar.

Now holds the work the team is doing. It is a firm commitment. Next holds what the team expects to do afterwards. It's likely, but it may change. Later holds what the team is exploring. It's ordered by current thinking and promised to nobody.
Each item is written as an outcome, meaning a change in what people can do, and not as a feature. Under each item are a few lines of detail. Here is her entry for the first item.

Table 6.1: Anaya's roadmap entry for the first item. Outcome. Entry: Support staff no longer see identity numbers or tax numbers in the chat, and neither do the exports. Evidence. Entry: 37 of 400 conversations in one week; five interviews. Owner. Entry: Anaya and Imran. Depends on. Entry: Read access to the chat system; Lakshmi's sign-off. Kill criterion. Entry: Stop if agents switch it off in more than two of every ten chats within four weeks.
The last line was new to her. A kill criterion is a condition, decided in advance, that means the work stops.

It works for a psychological reason. After three weeks of effort, nobody is the right person to judge whether the work is going badly, because everyone has a reason to say it's going well. Written at the start, before anyone is attached to the result, the condition describes failure in words that nobody has to argue about later.

Kill criteria matter even more when the work involves software that reads and writes text. You can't know its accuracy in advance. You find it out by trying the software. So a date promised before the first test is a guess dressed up as a commitment.
Goals and the numbers beneath them.
Lakshmi's question was still on a sticky note on Anaya's desk. How would she know that the tool worked?

Companies answer this kind of question with objectives and key results, usually shortened to OKR. The objective says in words what you want. The key results beneath it are three or four numbers that show you got there.
Key idea: Outcomes, not outputs.

A key result measures an outcome, which is what changed for people. It doesn't measure an output, which is what was shipped. "Release the privacy tool" is an output: it can be done and nothing may change. "Fewer conversations leave the chat with a personal detail in them" is an outcome.

Anaya wrote one objective and two key results. The objective was to make Sahaj's support chat safe to export. The first key result was that the share of conversations leaving the chat with no unhidden personal detail would rise from 91 percent to 99 percent. The second was that support agents would report fewer than one chat in fifty in which the tool had hidden something they needed.
Two other kinds of number sit beside key results.

An input metric is a number the team can move directly, which you expect to move the outcome. For her it was the share of fixed-shape numbers the tool caught. You can't command the outcome, but you can improve the input.

A guardrail metric is a number that must not get worse while the team chases the others. It stops you from winning in a way that does damage. Hers was the false-alarm rate: the share of hidden items that weren't personal at all. A tool that blanked every number in every message would score perfectly on the first key result and be unusable. So she set the limit at three in a hundred.

There was one more distinction, and it was easy to lose once the work became technical. The tool would have its own score on its own test, and that measures the tool. The key results measure what happens to people. A tool can do well on its own test and still be ignored by agents who find it irritating, or arrive too late to matter. Both kinds of number were needed, and each had to be labelled as one or the other.
The people who can say no.
Imran asked who would actually read the plan. Anaya didn't know.

Anyone who can help or stop a project, or who is affected by it, is a stakeholder. And stakeholders are not all equal. So she drew a square with two axes: how much power a person had over the project, and how much they cared about it. Then she placed names in it.

Table 6.2: Stakeholders by power and interest. Power over it. Cares little: Keep satisfied: the founders, Lakshmi. Cares a lot: Work closely with: Imran, the head of support. Little power. Cares little: Keep informed: other product teams. Cares a lot: Keep involved: Farah's agents, customers.
Beside each name she wrote what the person was measured on, which tells you how they will react. She also wrote what they could decide: whether they chose, advised or could veto.

Lakshmi was in the wrong corner. She had real power and, as far as Anaya could tell, little interest. That combination is the most dangerous. People in security, legal and compliance often hold a veto while taking little part in the daily work. They stay quiet until the day before launch, and then they say no. They are usually right to.
The remedy was ordinary. Anaya moved her to the second column by visiting her every week and asking what she would need.
The decision memo.
The founders wouldn't read a plan. They would read the first paragraph of a memo, and perhaps the second.

A decision memo is written so that a busy person can act after reading only its opening. The order is: the request, the reason, the cost, the biggest risk, and the alternatives, including doing nothing. Here is Anaya's opening paragraph.
Worked example: Anaya's opening paragraph.

I am asking for Imran for half his time for eight weeks, and about forty thousand rupees in cloud costs, to build a small tool that hides personal details in our support chat before they travel any further. In one week of chats, 37 of 400 conversations contained an identity number, a tax number, a bank account or an address, and nothing removes them from our logs, exports or the outside company's systems. The biggest risk is that the tool misses things written in Hinglish. We will test it on real examples before it touches a live chat, and we will stop if agents turn it off in more than two of ten chats.
In four sentences, it states the ask, the evidence, the main risk and the stopping condition.
Imagining the failure.

Before the founders' meeting, Anaya held a gathering that Imran had dreaded and Farah had looked forward to. Everyone was to pretend it was six months later and the project had failed. Then each person wrote down, alone and without talking, why it failed.
This is a pre-mortem, and it works for a simple reason. People will name risks in an imagined failure that they wouldn't raise against a plan they're expected to support.

Farah wrote that agents had switched the tool off. It had hidden a customer's callback number in mid-conversation, and nobody had told them how to get it back. Lakshmi wrote that it had missed an address written in Hinglish, a screenshot had gone out in an export, and a regulator had asked how that was possible. Imran wrote that it had added a second to every reply, and customers had complained that the chatbot felt slow. Anaya wrote that the file of test examples had never been kept up to date, so nobody could tell whether the fourth version was better than the third.
Anaya turned all of this into a risk list.

Table 6.3: The risk list that came out of the pre-mortem. Agents switch it off. Likelihood: Medium. Damage: High. Owner: Farah. Response: Show agents what it hides and how to see it again. Misses Hinglish addresses. Likelihood: High. Damage: High. Owner: Anaya. Response: Test on real Hinglish before launch; narrow the scope if it fails. Slows replies. Likelihood: Medium. Damage: Medium. Owner: Imran. Response: Measure the added time from the first week. Test file goes stale. Likelihood: High. Damage: Medium. Owner: Anaya. Response: One person owns it; update on every change.

Beside it she kept a shorter list of things she needed from other people. A dependency is anything the project needs from outside the team: someone else's work, a supplier's cooperation, access to data, or an approval. Dependencies are where plans slip, because nobody on the team controls them.

Hers were three. She needed read access to the chat system, and she needed Lakshmi's sign-off before anything went live. She also needed a promise from the outside company that its software would not change how it accepted text. The first she could have by Friday. She was less sure of the third.
The outcome.
The founders spent eleven minutes on the memo. They asked how long it would take, how much it would cost, and whether Lakshmi had agreed. Anaya answered the third question first.
The decision went into the log she had begun on the first night, with a new line beneath it. She would change her mind if Imran's half-time could not be spared beyond week three.
A plan that other people can believe isn't one that sounds confident. It's one that has already told them how it might fail.
Chapter summary.
A roadmap that promises outcomes in Now, Next and Later columns breaks less often than one that promises features on dates. A kill criterion written at the start makes stopping easier.

An objective states the goal in words, and key results measure what changed for people. An input metric is a number the team can move directly, and a guardrail metric must not get worse. A tool's own test score is a different thing from a key result. Stakeholders differ in power and interest. A person with power and no interest is the one most likely to stop a project late. A decision memo opens with the request, the evidence, the main risk and the stopping condition. A pre-mortem asks everyone to imagine the failure first, and its output is a risk list with owners. Dependencies, which the team doesn't control, are listed separately.
Next, Anaya writes the whole thing down so that the engineers can build from it.
